$comment: One list of cases, read by BOTH implementations: `automationValidation.ts` (jest) and
`automation_validation.rs` (cargo, via include_str!). Two implementations of one rule set diverge
the first time only one of them is edited, and the divergence is silent — the editor greys a
toggle the backend would have allowed, or worse, the editor allows one the backend refuses and
the user's rule is rejected by a command they cannot see. `two-implementations-one-fix`.
Each rule is a COMPLETE AutomationRule in the wire DTO's own camelCase spelling, so Rust reads it
with `serde_json::from_str` and no adapter. Deliberately not a base-plus-patch shape: a deep-merge
would be a third implementation, present on both sides, that nothing checks.
`expected` is keyed on `code`, not on the message. One case is an uncompilable pattern, and Rust's
`regex` and the browser's `RegExp` word that error differently — a fixture comparing prose could
only be satisfied by weakening every case to a prefix match. Order is asserted too: both sides sort
blocking problems ahead of warnings, stably, so `expected` is the exact list in the exact order.

cases.name: the canonical rule is clean
cases.why: The rule this whole feature exists for. If this reports anything, the fixture is wrong.

cases.name: a pinned rule with nothing picked blocks
a pinned rule with a pick is clean even though its criterion is stale
cases.why: A pinned rule's criterion columns keep whatever they last held; nothing reads them.

cases.name: a criterion rule with no value to match blocks
all terminals needs no criterion value
a timer faster than the engine's floor blocks
cases.why: `due_now` clamps to 250 ms, so a rule asking for 100 would silently get 250.

cases.name: a too-fast interval is only a problem ON A TIMER
cases.why: `everyMs` is carried by an onOutput rule and never consulted — the scoped-default class.

cases.name: a timer at EXACTLY the engine's floor is clean
cases.why: Pins the constant itself, in both implementations. If either side's floor moves, one of them fails this case and the other fails the 100 ms one — which is what makes MIN_TIMER_MS a shared number rather than two numbers that happen to agree today.

cases.name: an empty pattern with a message does NOT warn about an echo
cases.why: An empty regex matches every position of every string, so an unguarded echo check told every half-built draft that its message matched a pattern it does not have. Found by writing this very case.

cases.name: an empty pattern blocks
a pattern of nothing but spaces is empty too
the Any number preset's decimal pattern is clean in both engines
cases.why: A preset only the browser can compile fills the field with a pattern `reload` refuses — a rule that saves, enables, and never runs. automationPresets.test.ts asserts every starter pattern appears here, so this case is what proves the Rust regex build too.

cases.name: the An error code preset's pattern is clean in both engines
an uncompilable pattern blocks, and reports ONLY that
cases.why: One cause, one message: a failed compile must not also report 'no brackets'.

cases.name: keeping the brackets of a pattern that has none blocks
the same pattern is fine when the whole match IS the value
a TEXT rule carrying keep:brackets is clean
cases.why: R8's own canonical rule. `keep` is numeric-only; blocking on it made the whole word-matching half of the feature un-enableable.

cases.name: more than one bracketed group warns without blocking
naming a group `value` answers the question the warning asks
a numeric rule with no operator blocks
a numeric rule with no threshold blocks
a TEXT rule needs neither operator nor threshold
an empty message blocks, and cannot also warn about an echo
cases.why: The echo check is the `else` of the empty check: an empty message matches nothing.

cases.name: a message matching the rule's own pattern warns
cases.why: §2.6's echo failure, told before it happens. The needle guard handles it, so it warns.

action.message: prepare to do a context hand-off

cases.name: blocks are ordered ahead of warnings, and each keeps its own order
cases.why: A caller that shows one problem shows the one that matters. The sort is stable, so the two warnings stay in emission order behind the block.

cases.name: a warning EMITTED BEFORE a block is still sorted after it
the mockup's five-problem draft reports exactly five, in step order
cases.why: §07's own screenshot. Every category the feature validates, in one rule.

cases.name: edge whitespace in the pattern is part of it, so this is not an echo
cases.why: The echo check used to compile `find.trim()` on BOTH sides, twelve lines under a comment forbidding exactly that. Trimming only ever widens the match, so this rule — whose pattern needs a leading space the message does not have — was warned about as an echo of itself. Both mirrors had the bug, so no fixture case could see it until one had edge whitespace.

cases.name: the same pattern against a message it really does match still warns
cases.why: The paired positive. Without it, `action.echo` could be deleted outright and the case above would still pass.

cases.name: regex's own `(?P<value>)` spelling is understood, not blocked
cases.why: `regex` keeps `(?P<name>...)` as a named group and RUNS it; V8 throws `Invalid group`. The editor blocked the Enable toggle and printed `That pattern could not be understood` for a pattern the authority would run — the strict direction `automationValidation.ts` says cannot happen. Two groups with none named `value` would warn; naming one is what suppresses it, so this case pins the rescue AND the name detection.

cases.name: action.unknownToken — $3 with two groups
cases.why: Two groups exist, but the message asks for a third. `substitute` is opt-in (plan 032 §4.2), so a text rule can carry this pattern and message with the toggle off with nothing wrong — the case right after this one.

cases.name: no problem when substitution is off
cases.why: The same $1 that would be a token with `substitute` on is the literal `awk '{print $1}'` people already write — opt-in is what keeps it working.

cases.name: $$1 is escaped, not a token
cases.why: The scanner shared with `subst.rs` treats `$$` as an escaped literal dollar, so `$$1` never reaches the token check at all, whatever the pattern can supply.

cases.name: action.tokenWithoutParse — substitute is on but there is no pattern
cases.why: The toggle says the message means to insert a capture, which nothing can be true of before a pattern exists — asked regardless of whether a token has actually been typed yet, the same way `cond.incomplete` is asked regardless of what a clause would compare against.

cases.name: action.unknownToken — ${bogus} when the pattern has no such name
cases.why: The named branch of the token check (`!names.has(t.name)`) had no case of its own — only the positional `$3` case above did. A named lookup for a group the pattern never declares must block exactly like an out-of-range number does.

cases.name: substitute is on, the pattern exists, and the message names no token
cases.why: The one shape neither validator's fixture pinned: `substitute` true with a real pattern, but a message that never asks for a capture. There is nothing for `tokensUsed` to walk, so nothing should block.

cases.name: cond.unknownToken — a clause sources $2 beyond the pattern's group count
cases.why: Plan 032 §8. Same predicate as `action.unknownToken` (`token_supplied`/`tokenSupplied`), applied to a clause's `Source` instead of a message token — one group exists, the clause asks for a second.

cases.name: cond.unknownToken — a clause sources ${bogus} the pattern has no group for
cases.why: The named branch of the same predicate: the pattern declares no name at all, so `${bogus}` cannot be legal in a clause any more than it would be in a message.

cases.name: cond.clauseNeedsValue — a text clause with no text
cases.why: `contains` is not in the `isEmpty`/`isNotEmpty` exception, so an empty `value` cannot be compared against anything.

cases.name: cond.clauseNeedsValue's exception — 'is empty' needs no text
cases.why: The paired positive: without this, the check above could be an unconditional 'value must be non-empty' that would also block the one operator the spec explicitly exempts.

cases.name: cond.badClausePattern — a matches clause whose own regex will not compile
cases.why: One grammar, one compiler (`compile`/`compilePattern`) — the same one that checks the rule's own pattern also checks a `matches` clause's, so there is no second regex parser to disagree with the first.

cases.name: cond.clauseWithoutParse — a clause on a rule with no pattern
cases.why: A schedule rule has no pattern to capture from at all; today that is approximated by a blank `find`, which `parse.empty` already blocks — this is the SECOND, independent fact that the cond panel also has something to fix.

cases.name: an empty clause list is legal — fire on the match
cases.why: Plan 032 §5.4: empty `clauses` is not a special case invented for this milestone, it is R8's existing text rule written down. A validator that blocked it would break every rule that fires on a bare match today.
